# Storage and moving data

The three filesystems, what each one promises, how to get data in and out, and ARCC's S3 object
storage.

## Where your data lives {#sec-storage}

### Nothing is backed up

**Nothing on MedicineBow is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch.**

There *are* snapshots (point-in-time copies; within about 20 days you can ask
`arcc-help@uwyo.edu` to restore from one), but they live on
the **same storage array** as your live data — if the array fails, the snapshots fail with
it. Snapshots protect against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Anything you can't
afford to lose needs a copy elsewhere: your institution's storage, a cloud bucket, an ARCC S3
bucket (separate hardware, but also not backed up; @sec-s3), or the separate **Alcova**
service, which does have real nightly backups.

### The three filesystems

| Path | Quota | Snapshots | Backups | Purged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/home/$USER` | **50 GB** | yes | **NO** | only when you leave UW |
| `/project/<project>` | **5 TB** | yes | **NO** | 6 months after project ends |
| `/gscratch/$USER` (`$SCRATCH`) | **5 TB** | yes | **NO** | **after 90 days of inactivity** |
| `/project/<project>/software` | **+250 GB** on top of project | yes | **NO** | with the project |
| `/lscratch` | node-local, varies | no | **NO** | **wiped at the end of every job** |

Check your usage and limits for home, scratch, and project:

```bash
arccquota
```

#### `/home` — small, personal, for config not data

50 GB fills fast once a conda environment eats 15 GB of it. Home is for dotfiles, scripts,
and small configs — not datasets and not software installs. When home fills up, things break
(jobs fail to write logs, logins misbehave), so watch it with `arccquota` and
`du -sh ~/* | sort -h`.

#### `/project/<project>` — the shared workhorse

5 TB, shared by everyone on your project. This is where shared
datasets, inputs, and results belong. Agree on a directory convention with your group so you
don't clobber each other. It persists for 6 months after the project ends.

#### `/gscratch/$USER` — fast and disposable

Also 5 TB, and the **fast** filesystem — use it as the working directory for jobs with heavy
I/O. Files untouched for **90 days** are purged automatically. Never keep the only copy of
anything here.

#### `/lscratch` — node-local, gone when the job ends

Each compute node has its own local disk at `/lscratch`. It's the fastest storage available
to a job (no network in the way), ideal for scratch files a single job reads and rewrites
constantly. It's **wiped when your job ends**, so copy anything you want to keep back to
`/project` or `/gscratch` before the job exits.

### Install software in project space, not home

::: {.callout-important}
## Install software into `/project/<project>/software`, not `/home`
Your project has an extra **250 GB** quota at `/project/<project>/software` for installing
software. A single conda environment with a few scientific packages can be 10–20 GB — two of
those fills a 50 GB home directory.

Point conda, pip, R libraries, and manual builds at project software space from the start.
The conda chapter (@sec-conda) shows how.
:::

### A sane layout to adopt on day one

```text
/home/<you>/                      # dotfiles, small scripts, SSH keys
/project/<project>/
    software/                     # conda envs, container images, manual builds
    data/                         # shared input datasets
    <you>/                        # your working area within the project
/gscratch/<you>/                  # active job working dirs, heavy I/O, big temp output
```

## Moving data in and out {#sec-moving-data}

### Pick the right tool for the size of the job

| Transfer | Best tool |
|---|---|
| Hundreds of GB / TB, or must-not-corrupt datasets | **Globus** |
| A few files, a script, a config | `scp` or `rsync` over SSH |
| To/from ARCC's S3 buckets | `rclone` (@sec-s3) |
| To/from other cloud storage (AWS S3, Google Drive, etc.) | `rclone` |
| Drag-and-drop a handful of files in a browser | Portal → Files |

There is **no dedicated data-transfer node (DTN)** — CLI transfers go through the login
nodes, and Globus manages its own endpoint. Another reason to prefer Globus for big moves: it
won't tie up (or get killed on) a shared login node.

### Globus — the recommended path for real data

[Globus](https://www.globus.org/) transfers between "collections" (endpoints). It's
restartable, checksums what it moves, retries failures, and runs server-side, so you can
start a multi-hundred-GB transfer, close your laptop, and get an email when it's done.

1. Log in at <https://app.globus.org> (choose "University of Wyoming" as your organization,
   or your own institution).
2. Search collections for **`uwyo-ARCC`** and pick **"Medicine Bow"**.
3. The Medicine Bow collection's root is **`cluster`**, so your project shows up at a path
   like `/cluster/medbow/project/<project>/...`.
4. Set the other side to your institutional or personal collection (install **Globus
   Connect Personal** on your own machine to make it an endpoint), pick files, and hit
   **Start**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Globus needs a full UW account
ARCC-Only accounts (external collaborators — @sec-account) **cannot use Globus.** If your
data lives at CSU, CU, or NCAR and you're on an ARCC-Only account, you'll need a UW-side
person to broker the transfer, or a **guest collection** set up for you.
:::

### `scp` and `rsync` — fine for small, everyday transfers

From your laptop, push a file up:

```bash
scp results.csv <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/<project>/<you>/
```

Pull one down:

```bash
scp <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/gscratch/<you>/output.nc .
```

`rsync` is better for directories and for resuming — it only copies what changed, so an
interrupted transfer picks up where it left off:

```bash
rsync -avP ./localdir/ <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/<project>/<you>/dir/
```

The `-P` flag shows progress and enables resume; `-a` preserves timestamps and permissions.
For more than a few GB, prefer Globus — a login-node `scp` of a huge file competes with
everyone else's login-node activity and will be slow.

### `rclone` — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)

`rclone` is ARCC's recommended CLI for moving data to and from cloud services. It's a module:

```bash
module load gcc/14.2.0 rclone/1.63.1   # rclone needs a compiler module first
rclone config          # one-time: set up a "remote" (S3 bucket, Drive, etc.)
rclone copy mydata/ myremote:bucket/path/    # copy up
rclone copy myremote:bucket/path/ ./mydata/  # copy down
```

`rclone` verifies and retries, and handles many small files far better than a loop of `scp`s.
For ARCC's own S3 service — setup, caching data for jobs, and access from Python, R, and Julia
— see @sec-s3.

### A quick decision guide

- **Moving your project's primary dataset onto the cluster?** Globus.
- **Iterating on a submit script from your laptop?** `rsync` (or edit in the portal).
- **Pulling results into a cloud bucket for a collaborator?** `rclone`; for ARCC's S3 service,
  see @sec-s3.
- **External collaborator without Globus?** Ask your UW PI about a guest collection, or share
  files from an ARCC S3 bucket with time-limited links (@sec-s3-link).

## ARCC S3 object storage {#sec-s3}

ARCC runs an S3-compatible object store on hardware separate from the cluster filesystems. You
reach it over HTTPS with an access key and a secret key: from login nodes, from compute nodes
inside jobs, and from machines off the cluster. ARCC suggests it for sharing data with
collaborators outside UW. This section covers getting a bucket, moving data with `rclone`,
caching bucket data for jobs, and reading and writing from Python, R, and Julia.

::: {.callout-note}
## Endpoint: `https://s3.arcc.uwyo.edu`
The service is a Ceph Object Gateway at **`https://s3.arcc.uwyo.edu`**, checked from login and
compute nodes in September 2026. ARCC's pages also call the service **Pathfinder**; the
hostname `pathfinder.arcc.uwyo.edu` does not respond from the cluster. If ARCC gives you a
different endpoint with your keys, use theirs.
:::

### How a bucket differs from `/project`

A **bucket** holds **objects**: a file's bytes stored under a key such as
`inputs/era5/2024-07.nc`. There are no directories; the slashes are part of the key, and tools
display them as folders. Programs reach objects through an S3 client or library rather than a
file path (except through a mount, @sec-s3-cache), and an object is replaced whole rather than
edited in place.

| | `/project/<project>` | ARCC S3 bucket |
|---|---|---|
| Access | file path | S3 client or library, with keys |
| Reachable from | the cluster | the cluster and off-cluster machines |
| Modify part of a file | yes | no — objects are replaced whole |
| Hardware | cluster storage array (shared with home and scratch) | separate Ceph cluster |
| Backed up | no | no |
| Cost | included with the project | charged at ARCC's hardware-cost rate |
| How to get it | comes with the project | separate request (below) |

Typical uses:

- A second copy of results on hardware separate from home, project, and scratch.
- Sharing data with collaborators outside UW, including those on ARCC-Only accounts that can't
  use Globus (@sec-account).
- Time-limited download links for individual files (@sec-s3-link).
- A reference copy of an input dataset that jobs pull from and people off the cluster can also
  read.

::: {.callout-warning}
## S3 is not backed up either
ARCC states that the S3 service is not backed up. A copy in S3 is on different hardware from
home, project, and scratch, so it is not lost if the cluster's storage array fails, but it is
still a single copy. Data you can't regenerate needs a copy outside ARCC as well.
:::

### Getting a bucket and keys

1. **Request it** with ARCC's research project request form, and state in the description that
   you are requesting the S3 service. ASCEND/ARID performers: ask your team or Virginia
   Iglesias (@sec-account) first whether your project already has a bucket.
2. **Save the keys when they arrive.** After approval, ARCC replies with a temporary link,
   active for a few days, to an **access key** and a **secret key**. Store both in a password
   manager. Anyone with both keys has full access to your buckets.
3. **Buckets:** ARCC creates one bucket for the project, and your keys can create one more (two
   total). Ask ARCC if you need more.

Charges cover hardware cost only; ARCC and UW's Office of Research and Economic Development
subsidize staff and datacenter costs. Rates are in the
[ARCC Cost Policies](https://www.uwyo.edu/arcc/policies/costpolicy.html).

On a laptop, ARCC supports `rclone` and MSP360 Explorer (a Windows/macOS GUI); Cyberduck,
Transmit, and `s3cmd` are best-effort.

### Set up `rclone` once {#sec-s3-rclone}

`rclone` is installed as a module and is ARCC's supported command-line client. Create a remote
named `arccs3`. Reading the keys with `read` keeps them out of your shell history:

```bash
module load gcc/14.2.0 rclone/1.63.1

read -rp  "Access key: " AK
read -rsp "Secret key: " SK; echo
rclone config create arccs3 s3 provider=Ceph endpoint=https://s3.arcc.uwyo.edu \
    access_key_id="$AK" secret_access_key="$SK"
unset AK SK
```

This writes the remote to `~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf`, with permissions that let only you
read it. The keys are stored there in plain text; don't copy that file into a Git repository or
a shared directory. On a laptop, `rclone config` prompts for the same values: storage type
`s3`, provider `Ceph`, your two keys, and the endpoint.

Check the connection:

```bash
rclone lsd arccs3:                 # your buckets
rclone lsf arccs3:<bucket>         # top level of a bucket
rclone size arccs3:<bucket>        # object count and total size
```

`InvalidAccessKeyId` means the access key is wrong; `SignatureDoesNotMatch` means the secret key
is wrong. Run the `rclone config create` step again with the right keys; it overwrites the
remote.

### Upload and download

A remote path is `arccs3:<bucket>/<key prefix>`. `rclone copy` sends only files that are missing
or differ (by size and modification time) at the destination, so re-running an interrupted copy
skips what already arrived.

```bash
# upload a directory
rclone copy /project/<project>/<you>/results arccs3:<bucket>/results -P

# download a prefix
rclone copy arccs3:<bucket>/inputs/era5 /gscratch/$USER/era5 -P

# one file, to an exact key
rclone copyto summary.csv arccs3:<bucket>/results/summary.csv

# after a large transfer, confirm both sides match
rclone check /project/<project>/<you>/results arccs3:<bucket>/results
```

`-P` shows live progress.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `rclone sync` deletes files
`rclone sync SRC DST` makes `DST` match `SRC`, **deleting** anything in `DST` that isn't in
`SRC`. With the arguments reversed, it deletes the data you meant to keep. Use `copy` unless you
need deletions, and run `sync` with `--dry-run` first.
:::

#### Large transfers

- **Run them in a job**, not on a login node — there is no data-transfer node
  (@sec-moving-data), and compute nodes can reach the S3 endpoint.
- **Many small files:** raise `--transfers` (files in parallel, default 4) and `--checkers`
  (comparisons in parallel, default 8). Each object is a separate HTTPS request, so for hundreds
  of thousands of small files, pack them into a `tar` archive first.
- **A few large files:** raise `--s3-chunk-size` (default 5 MiB) and `--s3-upload-concurrency`
  (default 4) to send more of each file in parallel. `rclone` holds `--s3-upload-concurrency`
  chunks in memory for each file it is transferring, so size `--mem` to match.

A transfer job:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<project>
#SBATCH --job-name=s3-upload
#SBATCH --partition=mb
#SBATCH --qos=fast
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=s3-upload-%j.out

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 rclone/1.63.1

rclone copy /project/<project>/<you>/archive arccs3:<bucket>/archive \
    --transfers 16 --checkers 16 \
    --stats 5m --stats-one-line --stats-log-level NOTICE
```

The `--stats` flags write a one-line progress report to the job log every five minutes. Without
`--stats-log-level NOTICE`, `rclone` doesn't print them at its default log level.

### Share a file with a time-limited link {#sec-s3-link}

`rclone link` creates a presigned URL: anyone with the URL can download that object, without
keys, until it expires.

```bash
rclone link --expire 72h arccs3:<bucket>/results/summary.csv
```

S3 presigned links last at most 7 days; `rclone` shortens longer requests to 7 days.

### Caching bucket data for jobs {#sec-s3-cache}

Each read from a bucket is a network request. A job that reads the same objects repeatedly, or
an array whose tasks each download the same inputs, spends time waiting on the network and adds
load to a shared service. Download the data to cluster storage once and have jobs read local
files. The bucket stays the source of truth; the local copy is a cache you can delete and
rebuild.

#### A persistent cache on `/gscratch`

```bash
CACHE=/gscratch/$USER/s3cache/<bucket>
rclone copy arccs3:<bucket>/inputs "$CACHE/inputs"
```

Re-running the command downloads only objects that are new or changed since the last run. Run it
before submitting a job array (@sec-arrays) and point the tasks at `$CACHE`; running it inside
every task repeats the bucket listing once per task. `/gscratch` purges files untouched for 90
days (@sec-storage); the same command rebuilds whatever was purged.

#### Stage to `/lscratch` for I/O-heavy jobs

Copy inputs to the node-local disk at the start of the job, and send results to the bucket at
the end:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<project>
#SBATCH --job-name=s3-stage
#SBATCH --partition=mb
#SBATCH --qos=fast
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --output=s3-stage-%j.out

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 rclone/1.63.1 python/3.12.0

WORK=/lscratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID
mkdir -p "$WORK"

rclone copy arccs3:<bucket>/inputs "$WORK/inputs"      # or copy from your /gscratch cache
python run_model.py --input "$WORK/inputs" --output "$WORK/output"

# keep the results on /gscratch if the upload fails
rclone copy "$WORK/output" arccs3:<bucket>/results/$SLURM_JOB_ID \
    || cp -r "$WORK/output" /gscratch/$USER/output-$SLURM_JOB_ID
rm -rf "$WORK"
```

#### Mount a bucket with a local cache

`rclone mount` presents a bucket as a directory, for programs that need a file path or read only
parts of large files. With `--vfs-cache-mode full`, the parts a program reads are saved to local
disk, and later reads of those parts don't go over the network. Mount inside a job, on
node-local disk:

```bash
MNT=/lscratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID/mnt
CACHE=/lscratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID/cache
mkdir -p "$MNT" "$CACHE"

rclone mount arccs3:<bucket> "$MNT" --daemon --read-only \
    --vfs-cache-mode full --cache-dir "$CACHE" --vfs-cache-max-size 100G
trap 'fusermount3 -u "$MNT"; rm -rf "/lscratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID"' EXIT

python analyze.py "$MNT/inputs/era5/2024-07.nc"
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Always pass `--cache-dir`
The default `rclone` cache directory is `~/.cache/rclone`, inside your 50 GB home quota
(@sec-storage). A `--vfs-cache-mode full` mount without `--cache-dir` can fill home.
`--vfs-cache-max-size` limits how large the cache grows.
:::

Use `rclone copy` when programs read whole files; use a mount when they read small parts of
large files, or when downloading everything first isn't practical.

### From Python, R, and Julia {#sec-s3-code}

S3 libraries work with ARCC's service once pointed at the endpoint. Put the keys in the standard
AWS environment variables, in a file only you can read:

```bash
touch ~/.arcc-s3 && chmod 600 ~/.arcc-s3
nano ~/.arcc-s3
```

```bash
# ~/.arcc-s3
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<access key>
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret key>
```

Run `source ~/.arcc-s3` in your shell before starting Python, R, or Julia, and in submit scripts
that use these libraries. Each example downloads an object into a `/gscratch` cache the first
time it's requested, reuses the local file after that, and uploads a result. The download goes
to a temporary name and is then renamed, so parallel tasks never read a partial file.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Python

ARCC has tested `boto3`. Install it with `certifi` in a virtual environment in project space
(@sec-pkgdirs): `pip install boto3 certifi`.

```python
import os
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="https://s3.arcc.uwyo.edu")
CACHE = os.path.join("/gscratch", os.environ["USER"], "s3cache")

# Local path to s3://bucket/key, downloaded on first use
def cached(bucket, key):
    path = os.path.join(CACHE, bucket, key)
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)
        s3.download_file(bucket, key, path)  # writes a temporary file, then renames it
    return path

with open(cached("<bucket>", "inputs/stations.csv")) as f:
    stations = f.read()

s3.upload_file("output/summary.csv", "<bucket>", "results/summary.csv")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`
Without `certifi` installed, `boto3` uses its own bundled list of certificate authorities, which
lacks the root that `s3.arcc.uwyo.edu`'s certificate chains to, and every request fails with
`SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`. Install `certifi`, or point `boto3` at the system list with
`export AWS_CA_BUNDLE=/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt`.
:::

#### R

ARCC has tested `aws.s3`. Install it with `install.packages("aws.s3")` after setting
`R_LIBS_USER` (@sec-pkgdirs).

```r
library(aws.s3)
Sys.setenv(AWS_S3_ENDPOINT = "s3.arcc.uwyo.edu")
cache <- file.path("/gscratch", Sys.getenv("USER"), "s3cache")

# Local path to s3://bucket/key, downloaded on first use
cached <- function(bucket, key) {
  path <- file.path(cache, bucket, key)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    dir.create(dirname(path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    tmp <- paste0(path, ".part", Sys.getpid())
    save_object(key, bucket = bucket, file = tmp, region = "")
    file.rename(tmp, path)
  }
  path
}

stations <- read.csv(cached("<bucket>", "inputs/stations.csv"))

put_object(file = "output/summary.csv", object = "results/summary.csv",
           bucket = "<bucket>", region = "")
```

`region = ""` is required: with the default region, `aws.s3` sends requests to
`us-east-1.s3.arcc.uwyo.edu` instead of the endpoint.

#### Julia

`AWSS3.jl` provides the S3 operations. `Minio.jl` provides `MinioConfig`, an AWS.jl
configuration for S3-compatible servers; it is named for MinIO, another S3 server, and works
with ARCC's Ceph gateway. Install both with `] add AWSS3 Minio` after setting
`JULIA_DEPOT_PATH` (@sec-pkgdirs).

```julia
using AWSS3, Minio

cfg = MinioConfig("https://s3.arcc.uwyo.edu";
    username=ENV["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"],
    password=ENV["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"],
)
const CACHE = joinpath("/gscratch", ENV["USER"], "s3cache")

# Local path to s3://bucket/key, downloaded on first use
function cached(bucket, key)
    path = joinpath(CACHE, bucket, key)
    if !isfile(path)
        mkpath(dirname(path))
        tmp = "$path.part$(getpid())"
        s3_get_file(cfg, bucket, key, tmp)
        mv(tmp, path; force=true)
    end
    return path
end

stations = read(cached("<bucket>", "inputs/stations.csv"), String)

s3_put(cfg, "<bucket>", "results/summary.csv", read("output/summary.csv"))
```

:::
